title: spiraling into your changing center
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

one of the most significant shifts I've ever had is letting go of linear (ladder-like) models of external success -- in order to put my own journey, process, and energy at the center. but, how do you do that, if you don't know what's at your center, or if your center is always changing?

I'll explore facets of this question through the metaphor of a labyrinth as journey -- how to dance with seasonal cycles, moving between structure and spontaneity, and focus on just taking the next step forwards.

a labyrinth as metaphor for the journey

today I want to talk about why movement through what you don't know is about spiraling inwards into a changing center. and the metaphor I love for this is the labyrinth, which is also the name of a seasonal community I recently opened. in that the crux of this is that our pathways and journeys are never linear. it's never about climbing one step after another on a staircase or a ladder, but instead about circling around the spiral of your being, of what you desire, of what you want to create in this world on a day-to-day basis. and so the practice of spiraling is about movement and centering. I want to talk about this movement a little bit today.

I think we've all been conditioned by a culture that says that there is a perfect map for what you want to do, that there is an approach, that there is a strategy for claiming the success that you want, something out there. if you just see how other people do the thing of making six figures or having a million subscribers on YouTube or monetizing AI or whatever it is, that there is an execution and why would you figure it out yourself? if you could just download, buy someone else's ladder, someone else's blueprint and follow it and climb it and get what you want.

I have definitely been guilty of this. I have paid thousands of dollars many years ago to follow someone else's plan and abandoned ship very quickly in and felt super ashamed and guilty about that. part of the work of being a creative person, figuring things out on the infinite space of the internet is recognizing that other people's plans, blueprints, programs, anything that prescribes a linear process may not always work for you. and I say may because sometimes I'm sure you will get so much, it depends on how you move through the world.

for me, I have trouble following other people's methodologies because my system resists, it's rebellious. and my journey has been all about being uncompromisingly true to myself, my own process and how I want to be and move, which is why I'm describing this journey through the metaphor of a labyrinth.

what is a labyrinth?

a labyrinth is basically a garden path that has a center that you spiral towards and there may be what seems like dead ends, but eventually if you follow the path, you will get closer to the center. I see this as a metaphor for the creative process, for journeying, as a metaphor for my work, my business, my website, where the focus is not on achieving or getting some outcome, the focus is completely on the process of movement. and through the process, you will find that as a byproduct, you will have created things and shared things and made some money.

the first workshop I share in Labyrinth Library, my community, is called Labyrinth as a Map for Wayfinding. and I remind everyone that we each have our own personal labyrinths. I have my own, you have yours, and they may look very, very different even if we have similar things that we desire at the center.

and so when you think about your labyrinth, some questions you could ask are what feels known versus what feels unknown, what variables are in my life that I'm thinking about right now? what is the mystery path? is there a central question or a mystery that you're investigating through walking the labyrinth? is there a puzzle?

I like to think of challenges as puzzles. some puzzles feel so impossible to solve. some puzzles, like the puzzle of art and money, has been a puzzle that I've been trying to solve for years and could feel the milestones of solving the puzzle in a very nonlinear embodied way. and even now, I could say that I've solved it, but more accurately, I'm in the process of discovering, of letting the puzzle teach me something new, of walking the labyrinth of that journey.

and ultimately at the center of the labyrinths of our lives is death. we're here for a brief period of time. we try to make meaning and find beauty and fulfillment and share something with those we share the journey with. and then we go somewhere else. and so perhaps this reminder is simply to be as present as you can with each step of the spiral and take a deep breath.

dancing around your center

the central premise of spiraling or the movement of spiraling, which can sound negative when it's applied to like anxiety spirals, is that it is the work, the movement of dancing around a center of your center is the day-to-day practice and process. and here I would ask you questions. what do you feel is at the center of your labyrinth? what are you spiraling around? what do you desire? how do you feel around in the dark? how do you practice holding yourself when you don't know where you're going or who you are?

and what if the center changes? what if you believe you want something now and then next week or next month, you find that you want something different?

I also find myself questioning sometimes why am I repeating the same spirals? why am I going in circles, in cycles again and again? and I think that the things which truly matter to us, which lay at the center of our spiraling labyrinths, our themes and topics and subjects that we can never find too much distance from, we can only see different facets of it and engage with different parts of it at different seasons of our lives, even if at certain periods, it feels like it's in hibernation.

and so perhaps part of the work of spiraling is embracing the seasonal relationships that you might have in relationship to different parts of yourselves, which parts are in hibernation versus which parts are being rebirthed or looking for more energy and momentum and expression, how your art, your practice, your relationship to place, to your process, to your work, to the internet, to your community, to your audience, all of that goes through seasons. and not everything is in active summer mode all the time.

the changing center

so each time you reorient yourself in the labyrinth in the spiraling pathway, it's anchoring as a practice what is at your center in this season.

in a certain season of my life, I supported myself through doing web design work, and then I allowed myself to be completely free flow, expressive, random, but showing up every day on my website to write about something as like a public creative notebook practice. in this season of my life, I'm thinking about how I can be more present and quote unquote consistent in my podcasting and newsletter writing practice and show up consistently in my community. so my center of my labyrinth changed from a two-pronged sort of approach of making money versus creative expression to something that's feeling more integrated and more about building stability and foundation in my digital ecosystem.

and I think we can allow our centers to shift naturally, to know that when you are taking the next step to what you desire at the center, the labyrinth itself, the spiraling pathway itself will shift and then a new center could emerge. so it's like there's doors within doors, there's centers internested within new centers. the destination is always changing.

taking the next step

so how do you complete a cycle of movement? how do you take the next step forwards? I used to be very much an overplanner, but the problem with nonlinear spiraling paths is that you can't really plan or try to optimize your schedule because you as a fluid being are always changing and the things that you feel energy for can be changing and hard to predict.

so instead of trying to create the perfect system, what I've been working through is starting with the intention, taking a pause before you begin to gather the energy, practicing the movement, whether that's 30 minutes writing something or sharing something or sending a newsletter, and then allowing yourself to arrive, to complete, to be at stillness. you can break down what feels like a thorny, tangled, wild labyrinth path into the steadiness of daily movements.

so when we ask, how do I move at uncertainty? the questions that then come to me are, what movements, what practices feel safe? what movements or practices feel possible? how can you un-paralyze yourself by doing one thing, even if that's just sending one email, posting one thing, sending one letter? and then how do I re-center myself?

because in order to have the energy to do hard things, it's so crucial to feel grounded and regulated. I think of the body as compass, as anchor, give yourself plenty of grounding practices, stillness, meditation, as well as movement practices, walks, spaciousness for your mind to wander on the page, and practice centering in what you know, in what you value and what you believe in, as well as centering in what you don't know to see perhaps a labyrinth in the spiral of your life as centered in mystery. what if that could be exciting instead of terrifying?

structure and flow

on a day-to-day basis, I find myself navigating this tension between structure and flow, between having containers that make me feel held, grounded, anchored, having systems and practices, and tiny pieces of certainty in what I'm working on and what I believe in and what I'm bringing to the page, or a unit of time, 30 minutes to be with this notebook, or a two-hour practice where I hit publish no matter what, and simultaneously the spontaneity and the movement that happens in that container, sensing into what wants to come, allowing yourself to be carried away by the wind or the water or whatever element you're feeling, and allowing flexibility so you can create those containers of time, of space, of practice, and you can let the path unfold. that to me is what one step forwards looks like.

and in that tension between structure and safety and groundedness versus spontaneity, I also see the image of a kite where you have something anchoring you down, holding you to the earth, and you have a sense of freedom, of motion, of discovery. and so the questions I would ask are, how can I feel safe, grounded, and held? and where do I long to expand, discover, and explore?

between this tension of safety versus expansion is the center of what you desire, of where you want to go, of how you want to be. that is the journey of the spiraling path inside the labyrinth.

the beauty of the path

and the beauty of this path is that for me, many years walking the labyrinth, I don't get bored. I feel like I'm not putting myself into boxes, forcing myself to climb ladders. I'm always in a dance with life and my creative energy, and thinking about what new worlds, what new creations I can bring, what new parts of me I can express and discover.

there's never really an arrival, there's only a becoming. or maybe there are arrivals, but they happen in smaller containers of time. you continually arrive and depart, arrive and depart.

sometimes when I'm feeling really philosophical, I talk to my friends and tell them how I love airports. not that airports are spiraling, even though they feel very labyrinth-like sometimes. and how I feel like sometimes life is like one big airport where we came from somewhere and we will go somewhere. and who knows where those places are, we're in the liminal space right now.
